Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Assertiveness: never disagree or assert myself to avoid conflict, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Hopelessness: I have no future, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Boun had spent forty-five years on the roofs of America, his body a testament to a life of hard labour under an open sky. At sixty-six, he was still strong, his hands calloused but steady. That strength, however, felt like a memory from another lifetime now. It had been seven months since the accident on a flat commercial roof in the city. The job involved a new sealing compound, a powerful solvent he’d never used before. The warning label was dense with text, and in the rush to beat the afternoon rain, his younger colleague had knocked over the industrial drum. The fumes were acrid and immediate, a thick, chemical cloud that caught in his throat. He remembered a searing pain in his lungs, the world tilting sideways, and then nothing until he woke to the sterile chill of a hospital room.

The first thing he registered was the darkness, punctuated by the rhythmic beep of a machine. A tube was down his throat, and a profound, suffocating terror gripped him. He was pinned, unable to speak or move, the antiseptic smell of the room filling his senses with each forced breath from the ventilator. That moment has become the lens through which he now sees the world. His memories of the trauma are not hazy; they are brutally clear, playing in his mind like a film he cannot shut off. He sees the white drum toppling in slow motion, the glint of the viscous liquid spreading across the black tar paper, the panicked look on the young man’s face. Sometimes, though, there is no image at all. He’ll be sitting in his armchair in the evening, and suddenly the raw, speechless terror of waking up in that ICU bed will wash over him, his heart hammering against his ribs for no reason he can name.

In the weeks and months that followed, Boun’s world began to shrink. He had come to believe it was a fundamentally dangerous place, a landscape of hidden threats he could no longer anticipate. He started turning down jobs in unfamiliar parts of the city, telling his wife the drive was too long. The truth was that he couldn't bear the thought of a new site, a new crew, new materials—too many variables he couldn’t control, too many chances for another disaster. Even on familiar jobs, his focus would shatter. Mid-hammer swing, the scent of tar remover would transport him back, and he’d lose his concentration, his grip faltering. He became convinced he couldn't rely on himself anymore, that his own body and mind were untrustworthy.

At home, the man his wife had known for four decades began to disappear. He tries so hard not to think about what happened, pushing the images down, but the effort leaves him perpetually exhausted and on edge. He is unable to relax, even in the safety of his living room. The smell of bleach when his wife cleans the bathroom sends a jolt of panic through him. He avoids any disagreement with her, any form of conflict, simply nodding and agreeing to whatever she says. It is easier than trying to explain the fear that coils in his stomach. This passivity has built a quiet wall between them. He spends hours just sitting, dwelling on how he used to be before the event: a man who could handle anything, who provided for his family without a flicker of fear. Now, he feels that man is gone forever. At his age, he sees no future, only this diminished, frightened version of himself.

It was his wife who finally insisted he seek help. Last week, he woke in the middle of the night, the bedroom pitch black, and was instantly back in the ICU. He scrambled out of bed, gasping for air, convinced the chemical fumes were filling the room. His wife found him crouched in the corner of the hallway, trembling and disoriented. The incident terrified them both. Boun is here now not with any great hope, but with a quiet desperation. He is afraid this fear will consume what little is left of his life, but a small part of him wonders if it’s possible to stand in his own home, in the quiet of the night, and feel safe again.
